where: Section 2, last paragraph ('When blocks are linear and time-invariant...')
problem: The text says series and parallel connections 'reduce to multiplication and addition of impulse responses'. In the time domain this is wrong: two LTI systems in series have overall impulse response h₁(t)*h₂(t) (convolution), not h₁(t)·h₂(t). Multiplication holds only in the transform domain, and no transform is named here. A student will carry 'multiply the impulse responses' into the exam.
fix: Say: 'When blocks are linear and time-invariant, a series connection has overall impulse response h₁(t)*h₂(t) (convolution), and a parallel connection has h₁(t)+h₂(t). In the Laplace or z domain these become the product H₁(s)H₂(s) and the sum H₁(s)+H₂(s).'

problem: 'A fixed over-amplifying system can be time-invariant and unstable' is misleading. A memoryless fixed gain y(t)=Kx(t) is BIBO stable for every finite K, however large, so the example does not support the (correct) point that stability and time invariance are independent. It also sits oddly with the earlier statement 'An audio amplifier with a fixed gain is stable'.
fix: Use an example that is genuinely time-invariant and unstable, for instance y[n]=2y[n−1]+x[n] (an accumulator with loop gain 2), or state clearly that instability needs feedback or memory, as in a feedback loop whose loop gain exceeds 1.

problem: The rule 'If only x(t) or only x[n] appears, the system is memoryless' does not cover scaled arguments. In y(t)=x(2t) or y[n]=x[2n] only the symbol x appears, so a student may wrongly call it memoryless, when the output at t uses the input at another time (2t) and is also noncausal.
fix: Add: 'Any argument other than plain t or plain n — a shift x(t−a), an advance x[n+k], or a scale x(2t), x[2n] — means the system has memory. Scaling or advancing the index also makes the system noncausal.'
